The judgment of the Court of appeals is reversed, and the case is 
remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.
Norton v. SUWA had immediate consequences in the lower courts and 
on agency action. A number of lawsuits pending in the lower courts were 
dismissed on the authority of Norton v. SUWA, and others challenging 
agency planning and management processes have subsequently been 
dismissed because they failed to identify a discrete agency action that the 
defendant agency was required to perform. See generally Noah Perch- 
Ahern, Broad Programmatic Attacks: SUWA, The Lower Courts^Responses, 
and the Law of Agency Inaction, 18 TUL. En v t l . L.J. 411 (2005).
The Forest Service also acted rapidly to capitalize on SUWA and an 
earlier decision, Ohio Forestry Ass'n v. Sierra Club, 523 U.S. 726 (1998), 
which held that federal land plans were generally not “ripe for review.” 
Citing both cases in the preamble to a new rule, the Forest Service 
emphasized the strategic nature of land management plans and 
characterized them as not authorizing specific projects, but as merely 
describing future desirable conditions and providing guidance for future 
decisions. National Forest System Land Management Planning, 70 Fed. 
Reg. 1023, 1025 (Jan. 5, 2005). The Service then revised the Forest Service 
Handbook to exclude all forest plans, plan amendments and plan revisions 
under its 2005 planning rule from NEPA requirements. Both SUWA and 
Ohio Forestry were cited as support for the view that land plans were only 
“strategic and aspirational” and thus could not have any direct 
environmental effects. National Environmental Policy Act Documentation 
Needed for Developing, Revising or Amending Land Management Plans; 
Categorical Exclusion, 71 Fed. Reg. 75,481, 483 (Dec. 15, 2006). For a 
further discussion of these matters see Michael C. Blumm & Shari L. 
Bosse, Norton v. SUWA and the Unraveling of Federal Public Land 
Planning, 18 DUKE En v t l . L. & POL’YF. 105 (2007).
C. TIMING

that a court wiR reach the merits. An agency decision may not be 
challenged prematurely, as gauged under the doctrines of “finality,”
